output_json.patch_notes:
Root cause: ExternalResourceHandler.getResource() and ClassPathResourceHandler.getResource() built the final on-disk/classpath resource location purely by string concatenation (addPaths(baseResource, UriPath.canonical(path))) and trusted that upstream URI-level normalization (Jetty-style UriPath.canonical, then Spring-style StringUtils.cleanPath inside the ExternalResource/ClassPathResource constructors) was sufficient to prevent the combined path from escaping baseResource. Those are two different dot-segment algorithms operating at different points (one before combining with the base, one after), and neither performs an explicit "is the final resource still inside the configured root" check — exactly the gap the alert calls out ("final resources must remain within their configured roots").

Fix: added `AbstractResourceHandler.isPathUnderBase(String baseResource, String resourcePath)`, a shared helper used by both handlers. It canonicalizes both the configured base resource and the fully-combined candidate path via `java.io.File#getCanonicalPath()` (which fully resolves ".." and platform separators lexically, independent of the earlier normalization passes) and requires the candidate to equal the base or be nested under it (`base + File.separator` prefix). Both handlers now call this check twice: once on the primary combined path (`addPaths(baseResource, path)`) before constructing the resource, and once on the welcome-file path (`addPaths(resource.getPath(), welcomeFile)`) before constructing the welcome-file resource — closing the same class of bug on the sibling ExternalResourceHandler/ClassPathResourceHandler call sites and the directory + welcome-file variant, not just a single highlighted trace. Because `ClassPathResource#getPath()` returns its path without a leading slash (by design, for classloader lookups) while `baseResource` is configured with a leading slash, the helper normalizes both sides with a leading slash before canonicalizing, avoiding a false-positive rejection that initially broke `ServletTest.testStaticWelcomeResource` (classpath welcome-file resolution) — caught by running the full suite and fixed before finalizing.

Two regression tests were added (one per handler) that stub `UriPath.canonical(...)` via PowerMock to return an escaping value directly, simulating any bypass of the upstream normalization, and assert `getResource(...)` now returns null instead of ever constructing/reading the out-of-root resource.
output_json.risk_notes: Low risk. The change only adds a rejection path (returns null, which the caller already treats as "resource not found" / 404) — it never changes behavior for paths that stay within the configured base resource. All 293 existing tests pass unchanged, including static-file integration tests (StaticFilesTest, GenericIntegrationTest, ServletTest, StaticFilesMemberTest) that exercise real classpath and external welcome-file resolution end-to-end. The canonicalization call (File#getCanonicalPath()) is a lightweight OS-level lexical/symlink resolution and only adds negligible overhead per static-file request (already dominated by disk I/O). One behavioral nuance: if a configured baseResource directory itself doesn't exist or symlink resolution throws IOException, the request is now rejected (caught by the existing broad catch-and-return-null block) rather than possibly succeeding before — this only affects misconfigured deployments and fails closed, which is the correct/safe direction for a path-traversal fix.
output_json.summary: Added a shared canonical-path containment check (AbstractResourceHandler.isPathUnderBase) that both ExternalResourceHandler and ClassPathResourceHandler now call before constructing/returning any resource — the first check on the base+request path combination, the second on the welcome-file path — so any resolved file that canonicalizes outside the configured static-resource root is rejected (returns null / 404) regardless of which upstream normalization step (UriPath.canonical, addPaths, StringUtils.cleanPath) failed to catch the traversal sequence, encoding, or platform-specific separator.
